# THEORYs with `tags` `learning-and-conditioning`

*Topics — What a work is about. Nucleation holds whatever reading the owner files here, whether or not an Anthology of the SOTA topic could also hold it; instruction for ML practice belongs to the anthology (ADR-048). The words are seeded from the clusters the reading-time triage of 2026-09-25 found, and grow by decision.*

**Learning and conditioning** — how organisms learn from contingencies and consequences — Pavlovian and instrumental conditioning, reinforcement and reward learning in brains, habit and goal-directed control, behaviour analysis and relational responding. Not machine learning, which is learning-theory or the anthology (ADR-025).

| [THEORY-044](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-044.md) v2 | In relational frame theory the self is verbal behaviour's content, its process and its context, and the self as context is a perspective learned from deictic relations that cannot itself be found as content | Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) define three selves: the conceptualized self, the content of verbal relations about oneself; the knowing self, their ongoing process; and the transcendent self, their context. Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) say the third arises from deictic frames (I–you, here–there, now–then) as "a sense of self as a locus or perspective", and is "a context for verbal knowing, not the content", so its limits "cannot be consciously known". The account maps the three onto the record's holdings: the content is the narrative self (Dennett, Gallagher, Strawson), and the context is what Hume could not find among his perceptions and what Metzinger calls a transparent perspective. It differs from the minimal self (Gallagher) on origin: RFT says the perspective is learned in language. The evidence for the learned origin is cited, not read, so Proposed. The clinical claim is [THEORY-051](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-051.md). | Proposed |
| [THEORY-046](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-046.md) v2 | Expected tangible rewards for merely engaging in an interesting task lower later free-choice engagement with it | Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)): across 55 experiments, expected tangible rewards given for working on an interesting task lowered free-choice engagement after the reward stopped (d = −0.40; children −0.43, college students −0.21), and lowered self-reported interest less (−0.15). By their study-by-study account, Cameron and Pierce's rival analysis found the same for this contingency (performance-independent rewards, −0.29), while disputing nearly everything else. Their 2001 reply (LIT-562), read here, re-codes 145 studies and finds it again: rewards offered for doing an interesting task lowered free choice, −0.35 across 57 studies. Active: both sides of the dispute find this effect. | Active |
| [THEORY-049](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-049.md) v2 | Whether an external event lowers or raises intrinsic motivation depends on whether it is experienced as controlling or as information about competence | Cognitive evaluation theory, as tested by Deci, Koestner and Ryan (1999, [LIT-557](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-557.md)) and summarized by Ryan and Deci ([LIT-559](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-559.md)) and Deci and Ryan ([LIT-558](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-558.md)): rewards, feedback, deadlines and choice affect intrinsic motivation through their "functional significance". Controlling events shift the perceived locus of causality outward and undermine it; informational ones affirm competence and enhance it, but only with a sense of autonomy. The meta-analytic pattern fits, and controlling versus informational positive feedback differ by d = −0.78 in four studies. Mediation by felt control is untested for rewards. Its rival, Cameron, Banko and Pierce's account (LIT-562), finds rewards tied to a score or to beating others do not undermine. Neither side has tested mediation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-050](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-050.md) | Psychological inflexibility, in which verbal relations give private events aversive functions and make experiential avoidance a general strategy, is a transdiagnostic process in psychopathology | Hayes et al. ([LIT-555](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-555.md)) model psychopathology as inflexibility: cognitive fusion supports experiential avoidance, which narrows behaviour. Barnes-Holmes et al. ([LIT-541](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-541.md)) give the mechanism: once a word stands in derived relation to an event it can carry that event's aversive functions, so private events become worth avoiding. Kashdan and Rottenberg ([LIT-553](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-553.md)) find inflexibility across depression and anxiety in cognitive, behavioural and physiological systems, and say its causal role is unknown. The evidence is correlational, small, mostly self-report and mostly from the model's authors, and the meta-analysis that would test it ([LIT-543](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-543.md)) is unread, so Proposed. It is compatible with the loop account of disorder, not a rival to it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-062](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-062.md) | Model-based and model-free predictions both operate in instrumental and in Pavlovian learning, and which one controls behaviour follows their relative reliability, not the preference of a supervising system | Daw, Niv & Dayan ([LIT-580](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-580.md)) cast habitual and goal-directed instrumental control as model-free caching and model-based search, and let behaviour follow whichever estimate is less uncertain; simulations reproduce the effects of over-training, task complexity and reward proximity on devaluation. Dayan & Berridge ([LIT-584](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-584.md)) show from instant revaluation of a salt cue that Pavlovian prediction also has a model-based form, and suggest the same reliability arbitration there. Both controllers pursue the same ends; neither is the irrational one. The instrumental half is qualitative simulation; the Pavlovian half of the arbitration is a suggestion. Proposed. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-154](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-154.md) | Whether an expected tangible reward lowers or raises later intrinsic motivation depends on how tightly its stated contingency ties it to performance and success | Cameron, Banko and Pierce (2001, [LIT-562](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-562.md)), re-analysing 145 studies with contingencies coded by procedure. On interesting tasks, expected tangible rewards undermine later free choice when loosely tied to performance (for doing the task, for "doing well") or earned at less than the maximum; they do not when given for surpassing a score, and they enhance it when given for exceeding others. Read through social cognitive and behavioural theory: rewards tied to success carry competence. Proposed: the paper measures no mediator and pools control groups that differ in feedback. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-307](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-307.md) | Adaptation by trial and error in a large system finishes in a practicable time only if partial adaptations are retained, and retention requires that the system not be fully joined: parts must be separated, at least temporarily, by constancies, and where later learning shares parts with earlier learning it destroys it | Ashby (1952; 2nd ed. 1960), [LIT-787](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-787.md), read in [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md), Chs. 10–16. If all successes must occur at once, trials grow as (1/p)ᴺ; if each is kept once found, roughly as N/p. Keeping one needs no channel from what is still changing to what is already right, so a fully joined system, the Homeostat included, cannot accumulate; constancies cut a system into independent parts. Exact for the type-cases; the fit to brains is qualitative. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-324](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-324.md) v2 | A system adapts by trial and error to an environment whose effect on its essential variables it does not know only if a second feedback, through those variables, changes the parameters of its primary feedback; and if that feedback changes them whenever, and for as long as, an essential variable is outside its limits, every equilibrium the whole can reach is an adapted one | Ashby (1952; 2nd ed. 1960), [LIT-787](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-787.md), read in [NOTE-851](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-851.md). Necessity is deduced from the trial-and-error rule against a Black Box environment; sufficiency from the theorem that a whole is at equilibrium only where every part is. The Homeostat shows it in a four-unit linear machine. The parameter changes are blind, and the account says nothing about how long the search takes, which is the subject of [THEORY-307](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-307.md). | Active |

| [THEORY-489](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-489.md) | Chains of human function learners, each trained on the previous learner's responses, forget their starting function and in 28 of 32 families converge within a few generations to a positive linear function, the bias earlier studies report, whatever function trained the first learner; this is convergence to the learners' favoured function, not shown to be convergence to their prior | Kalish, Griffiths & Lewandowsky (2007), [LIT-820](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-820.md), read in [NOTE-616](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-616.md). 288 participants in 32 nine-generation chains, four starting conditions. 28 families converged to a positive linear function; 3 converged to the negative linear one and 1 had not converged. | [THEORY-688](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-688.md) | In an actor-critic learner that can choose temporally extended options as well as primitive actions, options that fit the task speed learning, while options with ill-placed subgoals slow it, and options that fit an earlier layout keep the agent from finding a newly opened shortcut, so hierarchy helps only with the right subroutines | Botvinick, Niv and Barto (2009), [LIT-581](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-581.md), read in [NOTE-451](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-451.md). | [THEORY-1184](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1184.md) | In three laboratory studies of healthy humans, offering a costless avoidance response for a stimulus never paired with the aversive outcome led people to use it, and withdrawing the response then raised their expectancy of the outcome for that stimulus; signalling of the response is a confound | The wide form [THEORY-920](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-920.md) held before the thirteenth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-920](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-920.md), Active, is its evidence. The old title's clause "though not their skin conductance or startle in the one study that measured them" is not kept: it read more into the review than it says, and [THEORY-920](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-920.md)'s note of 2026-10-30 says why. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1186](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1186.md) | Across computational studies of exploration in reward-based bandit tasks, mostly in sub-clinical samples and not yet replicated, directed exploration tends to rise with trait or cognitive anxiety and to fall with state or somatic anxiety | The wide form [THEORY-917](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-917.md) held before the thirteenth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-917](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-917.md), Active, is its evidence. The old title's last clause, that random exploration shows no relation to anxiety, is not kept: the review reports only that no study links them, and [THEORY-917](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-917.md)'s note of 2026-10-30 says why. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1189](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1189.md) | In laboratory avoidance learning in healthy humans, an avoidance response that remains available during extinction persists, in some participants for hundreds of unpunished trials, and keeps expectancy of the aversive outcome higher than in people denied it; the more effective and the cheaper the response, the slower it extinguishes | The wide form [THEORY-901](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-901.md) held before the thirteenth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-901](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-901.md), Active, is its evidence. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1190](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1190.md) | In a Markov decision process, an agent that evaluates actions as if it will fail to avoid danger at later steps, while in fact choosing optimally at each step, spreads threat value to states far from the danger and avoids early and widely, which reproduces qualitatively exaggerated threat appraisal, fear generalization and several laboratory findings associated with anxiety | The wide form [THEORY-915](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-915.md) held before the thirteenth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-915](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-915.md), Active, is its evidence. Zorowitz, Momennejad and Daw (2020), [LIT-1496](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1496.md), state it of Markov decision processes in general and show it in the environments they simulate. The inherited promote_when asks for data in people, which the paper leaves to future work. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1191](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1191.md) | In a simulated active inference agent, a habit learned by counting the agent's own state transitions and policy choices emerges from goal-directed behaviour, and once acquired it persists, and reinforces itself, after the reward is devalued, while an agent devalued before acquisition switches at once | The wide form [THEORY-923](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-923.md) held before the tenth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-923](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-923.md), Active, is its evidence. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1193](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1193.md) | How far fear falls during an extinction or exposure session, or across sessions, does not predict how much fear is expressed at follow-up, in animals, human laboratory samples and fearful human samples | The wide form [THEORY-921](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-921.md) held before the fourteenth status review narrowed it, kept as a Proposed reading by the [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind-1 sweep of 2026-10-30: the source asserts it, and [THEORY-921](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-921.md), Active, is its evidence. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1324](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1324.md) v2 | In Ryan, Mims and Koestner's experiment, the same expected reward for doing well left less later free-choice engagement when given with controlling feedback than with informational feedback, and in both styles less than no reward with the same feedback: the interpersonal style of a performance-contingent reward changes its effect, and the reward lowers intrinsic motivation even when the information it carries is held fixed | Ryan, Mims and Koestner (1983), [LIT-1970](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1970.md), read in [NOTE-1522](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1522.md) from the scan on the SDT site. One experiment, N = 96, n = 16 per cell, ANCOVA on initial interest. The framing effect is F(1, 89) = 4.25 and the reward effect against feedback-matched controls F(1, 89) = 4.34; recomputed from the cell means without the covariate, about 4.9 and 3.4 (p ≈ .07). Felt pressure was higher under controlling conditions; mediation was not tested. Proposed for replication and mediation. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1355](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1355.md) v2 | Gershman, Blei and Niv propose that animals in conditioning experiments assign trials to latent causes under a prior admitting an unbounded number of causes, so that extinction is learned as a new cause rather than erasing the conditioned one, and that renewal and the context-dependence of latent inhibition follow from this inference while hippocampal lesions and immaturity abolish them by preventing new causes from being inferred | Gershman, Blei & Niv (2010), [LIT-2011](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2011.md), read in [NOTE-1547](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1547.md). A Chinese restaurant process mixture over trials, inferred online by a particle filter, reproduces acquisition, extinction, ABA and ABC renewal and context-specific latent inhibition in simulation; with the concentration set to zero it reproduces the loss of context-dependence after hippocampal lesions and in young rats. Proposed: the support is qualitative simulation beside replotted data from other labs, with no fitted parameters and no quantitative comparison with rival models. The wording is the reader's; adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1356](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1356.md) | Collins and Frank propose that people learning stimulus–action rules by reinforcement spontaneously build latent task-sets cued by one input dimension, even when that structure gives no advantage during learning, so that a new context signalling an old task-set is learned faster (positive transfer) while a new context whose rule partly overlaps old task-sets draws errors that would be correct under an old task-set (negative transfer) | Collins and Frank (2013), [LIT-2012](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2012.md), read in [NOTE-1545](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1545.md). Proposed: positive transfer replicated across the paper's two experiments (N = 33, N = 35) but is modest (t = 2.37, p = .024 in Experiment 1), and the negative-transfer interaction was significant over the whole group only in Experiment 1, a trend in Experiment 2. The EEG follow-up re-analyses Experiment 2's participants, so it is no independent replication. The account is behavioural; it does not say people perform Bayesian inference over task-sets, which the authors disclaim, nor that the Chinese-restaurant reuse prior is what people use, which they leave untested. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1362](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1362.md) | Mathys and colleagues show that a hierarchy of any number of Gaussian random walks, each level setting the log-variance of the one below, inverts under a mean-field variational approximation to one-step updates of the same form at every level above the first; each mean update is a prediction error weighted by the ratio of the precision of the prediction below to the posterior precision, a value prediction error at the first level and a volatility prediction error above it | Mathys et al. (2014), [LIT-2015](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2015.md), read in [NOTE-1548](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1548.md). The Hierarchical Gaussian Filter's update equations for n levels: the same precision-weighted prediction-error form at every level above the first, a value prediction error at level 1 and a volatility prediction error above. Proposed until the updates are re-derived. It says nothing about how close the approximation is to exact inversion, whether the parameters can be recovered, or whether people learn this way. The wording is the reader's; adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1363](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1363.md) | In Kemp, Perfors and Tenenbaum's account, abstract inductive constraints such as the shape bias are higher-level parameters of a hierarchical Bayesian model, here the within-category variability and population feature distribution of a Dirichlet-multinomial, learned from a few labelled exemplars per category at the same time as the categories' own feature distributions, and once learned they let a single exemplar of a new category license generalization by shape | Kemp, Perfors & Tenenbaum (2007), [LIT-2017](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2017.md), read in [NOTE-1544](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1544.md). Learning a constraint is inference over a hierarchy's higher-level parameters (α, β): low within-category variability of shape is the shape bias. The model reproduces Smith et al.'s first- and second-order generalization qualitatively, with no new experiments, and misses the no-name condition. Computational level; the structure and top prior are given. The wording is the reader's; adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1364](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1364.md) | Collins, Cavanagh and Frank propose that the latent task-set structure people build incidentally during simple reinforcement learning shows in prefrontal EEG: a switch of the dimension a participant treats as context, but not of the other dimension, evokes task-switch potentials over lateral prefrontal cortex, and the size of the early switch positivity and the decoded attention to that dimension each covary across participants with how much they later transfer learned rules to new contexts | Collins, Cavanagh and Frank (2014), [LIT-2007](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2007.md), read in [NOTE-1550](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1550.md). Proposed: one sample, the participants of Collins and Frank's (2013) Experiment 2 (N = 35; 33 for ERP, 32 for classification), with several uncorrected topographic tests and an early-positivity window chosen from the grand average. The late switch negativity tracked the context dimension but did not predict transfer; the early positivity, absent at group level, and the decoder did (ρ = 0.5, ρ = 0.35), and agreed with each other only marginally. The context dimension is assigned from behavioural switch-costs, so the EEG does not read out the structure independently. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1365](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1365.md) | Mathys, Daunizeau, Friston and Stephan derive, by a mean-field variational approximation with each variational energy expanded to second order at the previous posterior mean, closed-form one-step updates for a hierarchy of Gaussian random walks whose step sizes are set by the level above; the updates take the Rescorla–Wagner form, their learning rate rises with the inferred volatility, and individual differences are carried by fixed coupling parameters | Mathys et al. (2011), [LIT-2016](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2016.md), read in [NOTE-1552](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1552.md). A derivation with illustrative simulations: closed-form trial-by-trial updates for a three-level hierarchy of volatility, of Rescorla–Wagner form, with a learning rate that is the agent's posterior variance and grows with its volatility estimate, and with per-agent coupling parameters standing for individual differences. Proposed until the updates are re-derived. It says nothing about how close the approximation is to exact inversion, or about whether people learn this way. The wording is the reader's; adopting it is the owner's call. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1385](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1385.md) | Martinengo and colleagues find that spaced digital education for health professionals improves post-intervention knowledge more than massed digital education does, with a small effect, and promotes clinical behaviour change, while the evidence for spaced over massed digital simulation for skills rests on two studies of low certainty | Martinengo, Ng, Ng, Ang, Jabir, Kyaw & Tudor Car (2024), [LIT-2102](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2102.md), read in [NOTE-1610](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1610.md): 23 trials, immediate post-intervention outcomes. It does not say that spacing improves retention of skills over months, nor anything about long non-use; and for simulation the abstract and body give different pooled estimates (SMD 1.15 and 1.24). Proposed: one meta-analysis over studies mostly at unclear or high risk of bias. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1404](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1404.md) v3 | Oskar and colleagues find that the evidence on procedural skill decay among emergency physicians cannot yet say how long a procedural skill lasts after competence: few studies make decay the primary outcome, almost none follow skills beyond a year, most rely on simulation and checklist scores and study trainees, and many required procedures are unstudied | Oskar, Prehoda, Sapp, Qi, Botticelli & Palaganas (2026), [LIT-2019](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2019.md), read in [NOTE-1612](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1612.md): a scoping review of 37 studies, with descriptive counts and no quality appraisal. It does not say that emergency procedural skills decay at any particular rate, or that they decay more than other clinicians' skills; it gives no rates at all. Its closing statement of what decay depends on is asserted, not shown. Active as one review's mapping of one specialty's literature; whether another review finds the same gaps is QUESTION-403. | Active |
| [THEORY-1424](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1424.md) v2 | Tatel finds that procedural skills with motor components decline roughly linearly with months of infrequent use, by about 0.06 to 0.08 standard deviations a month on average, losing about half of training gains within six to fifteen months, and that accuracy declines more slowly when a performance opportunity, most often an earlier retention test, falls in the interval | Tatel (2023), [LIT-2079](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2079.md), the PhD dissertation behind Tatel & Ackerman (2025), [LIT-2088](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2088.md); read in NOTE-1560. A random-effects meta-regression over 457 sources. The slopes are the article abstract's too; the half-loss ranges are the dissertation's (the article gives 6.5, 13 and 11 months). The practice moderator holds for accuracy only, and the author calls the moderators far from definitive. It does not say that decay is linear beyond a year, where data are few, or anything about organizations. Active as a report of one meta-analysis; whether an independent synthesis agrees is open. | Active |
| [THEORY-1521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1521.md) v4 | Macnamara and colleagues argue that when automation performs a subtask while the operator goes on doing the task, the operator's skill at that subtask decays from disuse, the cognitive part more than the procedural part, and may do so out of the operator's awareness, because the task itself is still done and still succeeds | Macnamara et al. (2024), [LIT-2224](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2224.md), read in full in [NOTE-1710](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1710.md). A theoretical perspective with no data of its own. The decay with disuse, and its being larger for cognitive tasks, are the cited literature's (Arthur et al.; Ackerman and Tatel); the selective loss in pilots is Casner et al. (2014), reported second-hand, without sample or sizes; the concealment is the authors' argument, not a finding. Read as a stand-in for Bainbridge (1983), [LIT-2225](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2225.md), on the skill-decay irony only; the paper does not cite her. It does not give a rate, a recovery time, or any test of its extension to AI assistants. | Active |
| [THEORY-1522](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1522.md) v2 | Ahn reads Bainbridge's ironies of automation as holding that automation takes the routine work and leaves the operator the atypical cases, recalls the operator at its failure, when the system is least predictable, and leaves the operator's manual and cognitive skills degraded from disuse; and, as his own remedies for medical education, he proposes building core skills in phases free of AI before AI is introduced, and simulations in which AI failures are injected | Ahn (2025), [LIT-2222](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2222.md), read in full in [NOTE-1713](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1713.md). The ironies are Ahn's paraphrase of Bainbridge (1983), [LIT-2225](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2225.md), which was not read: he quotes no sentence of hers and gives no page, so this is a THEORY about how she is read, and nothing here is put in her name. The remedies are his proposals for medical curricula, untested. A single-author commentary with no data. | Active |
| [THEORY-1545](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1545.md) | When automation performs a subtask while the operator goes on doing the task, the operator's skill at that subtask decays from disuse, the cognitive part more than the procedural part, and out of the operator's awareness, because the task itself is still done and still succeeds | The thesis the source asserts, split from [THEORY-1521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1521.md) when the twenty-eighth status review promoted the report of it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1521.md) holds that the authors assert it; whether it is true is this entry's question, under the condition [THEORY-1521](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1521.md) carried, word for word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1551](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1551.md) | Bainbridge's ironies of automation hold that automation takes the routine work and leaves the operator the atypical cases, recalls the operator at its failure, when the system is least predictable, and leaves the operator's manual and cognitive skills degraded from disuse | The reading of Bainbridge (1983) that Ahn (2025), [LIT-2222](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2222.md), asserts, split from [THEORY-1522](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1522.md) when the twenty-eighth status review promoted the report of it ([ADR-065](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-065.md); [ADR-047](../../../record/decisions.d/ADR-047.md) kind 1). [THEORY-1522](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1522.md) holds that Ahn reads her so; whether she says it turns on her text, which the record holds only as Unavailable ([LIT-2225](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2225.md)), under the condition [THEORY-1522](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1522.md) carried, word for word. | Proposed |
